title: Maps and Their Uses
tagline: Types of maps, the elements of a map, scale, direction and the measurement of distance

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The scale conversions and the three-figure bearings quoted here are the standard conventions used on Survey of India maps. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Define a map and state the elements that every map must carry.
Distinguish between the main types of map and give a use for each.
Convert between representative fraction, linear and verbal scales.
Give the cardinal and intercardinal directions and read a three-figure bearing.
Measure distance on a map and justify the method used.

overview.intro: A map is a drawing of a place on a flat surface, made to scale, that shows the position, size, shape and relative position of the features of the area. Because the Earth is curved and a map is flat, some distortion is unavoidable, and the smaller the scale of the map the more detail it can carry. Every map, whatever its purpose, must carry a title, a scale, a direction indicator, a key or legend, and the conventional signs used for the features shown. Scale is the ratio between the distance on the map and the real distance on the ground, and it is the element that allows a map to be measured. Direction is shown either by the compass points, by an arrow or by a magnetic north line, and distance is then read off the map using the scale and, where it matters, the actual route followed.

learn.title: What a map is and why we use one

blocks.text: A map is a simplified representation of the surface of the Earth drawn on a flat sheet. It shows the position of places, the shape of the land, the size of distances and the relative position of one feature with respect to another. A globe shows the Earth more truly because it is curved, but it is awkward to use for measuring and it can show only a small part of the world at a time. A map can cover a very large area on a single sheet, can be enlarged or reduced to suit the purpose, and can carry as much or as little detail as is needed.

items: A map is drawn to scale, so that distances on it can be measured.
A map is a simplified representation, so only the features that matter for the purpose are shown.
A large-scale map shows a small area in detail, such as a town or a building plan.
A small-scale map shows a large area in general terms, such as a country or a continent.
A map is a more convenient record than a written description of position, because it shows relative position at a glance.

items.text: Why is it impossible to show the whole world accurately on a single flat map?
items.note: The Earth is a curved surface and a map is flat, so some part must be stretched or squeezed. The less it is stretched, the larger the area a map can cover, but the smaller its scale and the less detail it can show.

items.text: How is a map different from an aerial photograph of the same piece of ground?
items.note: An aerial photograph is a true record of what was on the ground at the moment of exposure, so every object appears exactly as it is, down to the shadow of a single tree, and nothing is exaggerated or omitted. A map is a selection: the cartographer chooses what to show and what to leave out, uses a conventional symbol to stand for each feature, and can enlarge a small area so that it can be drawn in detail. That is why a map of a town can show every street, a pipeline and a footpath, while a photograph of the same town taken from the same height shows only the roofs.

blocks.text: Maps are classified by the purpose they serve and by the information they emphasise. A topographical map is the most detailed general map of a region, showing both the physical features of the land and the works of people. A physical map shows only the natural features. A political map shows the boundaries of countries, states and districts. Thematic maps show one particular kind of information, such as rainfall, population density or crop distribution, and they include distribution maps, flow maps and choropleth maps.

items: A dot map uses one dot to represent a fixed number of people or of a fixed quantity.
A flow map uses arrows of varying thickness to show the direction and volume of movement, such as of trade or of migrants.
A choropleth map shades areas in different tints to show the intensity of a variable such as rainfall.
An isotherm map joins places of equal temperature with a line.
A cadastral or land-use map shows the boundaries and use of individual plots of land.

blocks.text: Every map, whatever its type, must carry certain elements so that the reader can interpret it. These are the title, which states what the map covers; the scale; the direction, usually with a north arrow or a magnetic north line; the key or legend, which explains the conventional signs; and the conventional signs themselves. A large-scale map also carries a grid of grid lines, an index of places and often a statement of the magnetic variation between magnetic north and true north.

items.meaning: The heading of the map, stating the area covered and the purpose of the map.
The ratio between a distance on the map and the corresponding distance on the ground.
The box on a map that explains the meaning of the conventional signs used.
A standardised symbol used on maps to represent a feature such as a railway line or a church.
A network of lines, usually numbered, that divides a map into squares so that any place can be located by a grid reference.

items: The scale may be expressed as a representative fraction, as a linear scale drawn as a bar, or in words.
A representative fraction has no unit, because the same unit is used on the map and on the ground.
A linear scale is the most accurate form because the bar is measured on the map itself.
The direction is normally given by the compass points or by a north arrow; a magnetic north line shows the direction of true north for the year of the survey.
On a topographical map the grid, together with the key, is what makes the map useful for the accurate location of places.

learn.title: Scale and the measurement of distance

blocks.text: Scale may be written in three ways. A representative fraction, such as 1 : 250,000, states that one unit of length on the map represents the same unit multiplied by 250,000 on the ground; it is the only scale that works for any unit. A linear scale is a graduated bar drawn on the map. A verbal scale, such as '1 cm represents 2.5 km', states the relationship in words and is the easiest to read aloud. To convert a representative fraction into a verbal scale, multiply the number after the colon by the length of one unit on the map and express the result in the same unit on the ground.

blocks.caption: Table: converting a representative fraction into a verbal scale
columns: What 1 cm on the map represents
What 1 cm on the map represents

items.text: A map is drawn at a scale of 1 : 250,000. What distance on the ground is represented by 6 cm on the map?
items.note: Ground distance = map distance multiplied by the denominator, with both in the same unit: 6 x 250,000 = 1,500,000 cm = 15 km.

items.text: Two towns are 45 km apart on the ground. What distance apart will they appear on a map of scale 1 : 250,000?
items.note: 45 km = 4,500,000 cm. On the map the distance is 4,500,000 divided by 250,000 = 18 cm. The same working gives 4.5 cm on a map of scale 1 : 1,000,000.

items: Distance on the ground = distance on the map multiplied by the denominator of the representative fraction.
For measuring curved distances such as roads and rivers, a piece of thread or a strip of paper is laid along the route and then measured against the linear scale.
Straight-line distance between two places is the shortest distance between them, not the distance along a road.
The larger the denominator of a scale, the smaller the area covered and the greater the detail shown.
A scale of 1 : 250,000 is called an intermediate scale, between the large-scale 1 : 25,000 and the small-scale 1 : 5,000,000.

blocks.text: Direction on a map is given in one of two ways. The cardinal points are north, south, east and west, and the intercardinal points lie between them, that is north-east, north-west, south-east and south-west. A bearing is a more precise method of giving direction: it is measured clockwise from the north line in three figures, so north is 000 degrees and east is 090 degrees. On a map with a grid, direction may also be given as a grid reference, and on a map with a magnetic north line, the difference between magnetic north and true north is the magnetic variation.

blocks.caption: Table: the eight principal directions and their bearings

items: Bearings are always measured clockwise from the north line.
The eight principal directions are equally spaced at 45 degrees from one another.
On most maps the north line is at the top, so north is straight upwards and south straight downwards.
On a map with a magnetic north line, the magnetic north may lie to the east or to the west of the true north, and the angle between them is the magnetic variation.
The direction of the Sun at noon in the Northern Hemisphere is always towards the south.

figures.caption: Figure: The elements of a map
figures.description: A map carries a title, a scale, a direction indicator, a key or legend, conventional signs and, on a large-scale map, a grid and an index. Without these elements the reader cannot measure, locate or interpret the map.

figures.description: A large-scale map covers a small area in detail, a small-scale map covers a large area in general terms. 1:25,000 shows a city block, 1:250,000 shows a town and 1:5,000,000 shows a country.

keyPoints: A map is a simplified, scaled drawing of a place on a flat surface showing position, size, shape and relative position.
Topographical maps show natural features together with human features; physical maps show only natural features; political maps show boundaries.
Thematic maps show one theme, and distribution maps include dot, flow and choropleth maps.
The essential elements of a map are title, scale, direction, key and conventional signs.
Scale may be given as a representative fraction, a linear scale or a verbal scale.
At 1 : 250,000, 1 cm on the map represents 2.5 km on the ground.
Ground distance = map distance multiplied by the denominator of the representative fraction.
The cardinal points are north, south, east and west; the intercardinal points are north-east, north-west, south-east and south-west.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north in three figures; north is 000 degrees and east is 090 degrees.
A large-scale map has a small denominator and shows a small area in detail.
examFocus: Scale questions always require the same working: convert both distances to the same unit, then multiply or divide by the denominator of the representative fraction.
A question asking for a verbal scale wants the wording '1 cm represents ... km', not just a number.
When you are asked for the type of map, name the map and then state one feature that identifies it, for example that a choropleth map uses shaded areas.
For a direction question, remember that bearings are clockwise from north and are written with three figures.
For distance questions, say whether the measurement is a straight line or a route, because the method of measuring differs.

questions.prompt: Among the following, the map with the greatest detail is the one with the scale:
questions.explanation: The smaller the denominator of the scale, the smaller the area covered and the greater the detail shown. Of the four, 1 : 25,000 has the smallest denominator.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 1 : 5,000,000, which covers a whole country and therefore shows the least detail.

questions.prompt: On a map of scale 1 : 250,000, 1 cm on the map represents:
questions.explanation: 250,000 cm equals 2,500 m, which is 2.5 km. The working is to multiply the denominator by the length of one unit on the map and convert the result into the same unit on the ground.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 250 m, which is the value for a scale of 1 : 25,000.

questions.prompt: The box on a map that explains the meaning of the symbols used is called the:
questions.explanation: The key, or legend, lists the conventional signs and states what each one stands for, so that the map can be read correctly.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'index', which is the list of places and their grid references.

questions.prompt: The three-figure bearing of north-east is:
questions.explanation: The eight principal directions are equally spaced at 45 degrees, and bearings are measured clockwise from north, so north-east is 045 degrees. East is 090 degrees and south-east is 135 degrees.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 135 degrees, which is the bearing of south-east.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a map that shows the natural features of the land such as rivers, mountains and lakes as well as roads and settlements is called a ________ map.
questions.explanation: A topographical map is a detailed large-scale map that carries both the physical features of the land and the works of people.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'physical map', which shows natural features only and omits settlements and roads.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ratio between the distance on a map and the corresponding distance on the ground is called the ________.
questions.explanation: Scale is the element of a map that allows a measured distance on the map to be converted into a real distance on the ground.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'key', which explains the symbols rather than the sizes.

questions.prompt: State three differences between a topographical map and a political map.
questions.answer: A topographical map is drawn at a large scale and shows the relief and natural features of the land together with settlements, roads, railways and land use, while a political map is drawn at a smaller scale and shows the boundaries of countries, states and districts. A topographical map shows the position and shape of physical features such as rivers and hills, whereas a political map shows the position of capitals, cities and administrative headquarters. A topographical map carries a grid and an index for locating places precisely, while a political map uses different colours or tints for each administrative unit.
questions.explanation: The three differences should cover scale, the kind of information shown and the way places are located.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that a political map shows only boundaries, when it also shows capitals, cities and the seat of government.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would measure the road distance between two villages on a topographical map.
questions.answer: First identify the scale of the map and note whether it is a representative fraction, a linear bar or a verbal scale. Place a piece of thread or a thin strip of paper along the road between the two villages and mark the point on the map where the thread crosses each settlement. Straighten the thread against a ruler and measure its length in centimetres. Multiply that map distance by the denominator of the representative fraction and convert the result into metres or kilometres. The measurement must be made along the road rather than as a straight line, because the road may curve around hills and other obstacles.
questions.explanation: Measuring along the route with thread and then converting with the scale gives the true distance travelled.
questions.commonMistake: Measuring the straight line between the villages and calling it the road distance, which ignores the bends in the route.

questions.prompt: Explain why the scale of a map is essential and what happens to the detail shown when the scale is reduced.
questions.answer: The scale is what gives a map its measuring power, because without it a distance on the map cannot be converted into a real distance on the ground, and the map would be only a picture. If the scale is reduced, that is if the denominator of the representative fraction is made larger, the map covers a wider area but shows less detail, because the same sheet of paper is now standing for a greater distance. Features that cannot be drawn at the new scale are dropped or generalised, so a country map shows the main cities and rivers but not every street and tributary.
questions.explanation: Detail and area covered are in competition: enlarging the area covered necessarily reduces the detail.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that reducing the scale removes the map's accuracy, when in fact the scale is still exact for the area it covers.

questions.prompt: A map is drawn at a scale of 1 : 250,000. Express this scale in words, convert it into a linear scale in kilometres, and find the ground distance represented by a measured map distance of 4.8 cm.
questions.answer: In words the scale is '1 cm represents 2.5 km', because 250,000 cm on the ground equals 2,500 m or 2.5 km. For the linear scale, a bar 4 cm long represents 4 x 2.5 = 10 km, and it should be divided into five equal parts of 2 cm, each representing 2.5 km, with 0, 2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 marked. For the distance, the ground distance equals the map distance multiplied by the denominator: 4.8 x 250,000 = 1,200,000 cm, which is 12,000 m, that is 12 km.
questions.explanation: The same factor of 250,000 is used throughout, and the linear scale is built from the map distance that the reader will measure.
questions.commonMistake: Writing the verbal scale as '1 cm represents 250 km' by moving the denominator straight into kilometres without converting centimetres.

questions.prompt: A student writes that maps are useless for studying the physical environment because they cannot show the true shape of the Earth. Critically examine this statement.
questions.answer: The statement is only partly true. It is correct that a map is a flat representation of a curved Earth, so some part of the surface must be stretched or squeezed, and for that reason no flat map can show the Earth perfectly. It is also true that a map cannot show the real vertical relief of a landscape, which is why a section or a three-dimensional model is used for that. The conclusion, however, is wrong. A globe also distorts the Earth, because it cannot be scaled up or down and is awkward to use, and it shows only a small part of the world at a time. A map can cover a very large area on one sheet, can be produced at any scale, and can be drawn with exactly the features that the purpose requires. Most geographical study depends on comparing patterns over wide areas, such as rainfall distribution, drainage and settlement, and that is exactly what a map does best. The correct conclusion is therefore that neither the globe nor the map shows the Earth perfectly; each is a convenient simplification for a particular purpose, and the map is the more useful tool for most geographical work.
questions.explanation: A good critical answer accepts the valid part of the statement, shows that the globe has the same defect in a different form, and then demonstrates that the map is better suited to most geographical purposes.
questions.commonMistake: Simply dismissing the statement as wrong, which loses the marks for the valid observation about distortion.
